quotes.quote: we introduce AVMeme Exam, a human-curated benchmark of over one thousand iconic Internet sounds and videos spanning speech, songs, music, and sound effects.

Each meme is paired with a unique Q&A assessing levels of understanding from surface content to context and emotion to usage and world knowledge, along with metadata such as original year, transcript, summary, and sensitivity.
current models perform poorly on textless music and sound effects, and struggle to think in context and in culture compared to surface content.

AGI should also understand not only what is said or shown on the surface, but what is actually being communicated: the sarcasm in a voice, the emotion in a song, the sense of triumph or defeat in wordless music
Existing multimodal benchmarks primarily focus on standard ASR, sound and object recognition, and NLP tasks.
Even advanced multimodal understanding largely evaluates explicit content hearable or visible within audio or video frames.
Therefore, here we test whether MLLMs can understand audio-visual memes, to think and feel above audio and video content, and where they succeed or fail.

AVMeme Exam is a multimodal benchmark for testing whether multimodal large language models (MLLMs) can really understand audio-visual memes, the short, widespread clips you see every day on YouTube, TikTok, Bilibili, X, etc.

Beyond recognizing “what is said” or “what object is shown”, it evaluates deeper, richer multimedia knowledge and thinking: cultural context, implied meaning, induced emotion, use of audio/video, and world knowledge.

In total, we collect 1,032 audio-visual memes spanning more than ten languages and five sound categories, with their distributions shown in Figure 3.
Each meme consists of a video segment (URL, onset, offset) sourced from YouTube (86.1%) and Bilibili (13.9%), most exceeding one million views.
all clips are selected and annotated by 27 audio and NLP researchers, raised in the U.S., China, Japan, India, Middle East, and etc.
we prohibit political materials and explicit depictions of sexual, violent, hateful, criminal, or drug-related content
we prompt GPT-5.1 OpenAI (2025) for syntax and grammar fix of the summary, usage, and Q&A fields
AVMeme Exam was curated by 27 audio and NLP researchers affiliated with universities and companies in the US and the UK, aged between 22 and 35, the majority of whom are current PhD students.
A view count of at least one million is a soft requirement.
Each meme is trimmed to a short segment (1–30 seconds). At most two distinct memes may be extracted from the same source video.
AVMeme Exam is verified by nine human verifiers.

Nine human verifiers check every entry, reviewing all metadata fields: transcription, summary, usage, sensitivity, language, video integrity, and the multiple-choice Q&A, on a clip-by-clip basis, and return to contributors to fix if any issues are identified.
Q&As that all three models guess correctly are flagged as text_cheat, for which the strong text priors allow the LLMs to infer the clip or the answer without listening or watching.
The full dataset is denoted meme-full (1032 memes), and removing all text_cheat items yields meme-main (846 memes).

From meme-full to meme-main, the deaf-and-blind guessing accuracy drops from 34.7→20.4, 37.9→24.3, and 40.9→27.9 for Gemini 2.5 Flash, Grok 4, and GPT-5.1, respectively, showing that meme-main represents a more exclusive test of multimodal understanding.
For visual_cheat clips, we omit the visual input when evaluating audio–visual models.
Q&As are categorized into seven question types by human verifiers, ensuring consistent labeling while allowing contributors to draft Q&As creatively without prior constraints.
Audio Analysis focuses on what the sound alone reveals: prosody, rhythm, style, or other audible patterns.
Language Analysis tests recognition and parsing of the spoken words, including what is said and how it functions within a sentence or conversation.
Contextual Inference evaluates whether a model can understand the situation behind the clip: what the speaker intends, what they mean, or what is happening in the scene.
Emotion Analysis asks the model to identify the feeling expressed, based on tone, delivery, pacing, or the effect on the audience.
Humor & Popularity asks why a clip became funny, iconic, or widely shared.
Usage & Application focuses on how people actually use the clip as a meme: the situations it fits, the message it conveys, or the reaction it arises.
World Knowledge requires information beyond the clip, such as who the speaker is, the media it comes from, or what event or reference it points to.
All models receive the same prompt: question with randomly shuffled options starting from letter A.
Audio is converted to monaural 16kHz, and video is converted to 360p resolution (aspect ratio preserved) at one frame per second.
For GPT and Gemini, we create temporary copies of the audio and video files (tmp.wav/mp4) and upload them as bytes, preventing the models from cheating with file names.
We evaluate 19 state-of-the-art MLLMs
Gemini 3 Pro is overall the best model in our benchmark, which achieves an average accuracy of 76.6 (audio-only) and 80.0 (audio–visual) on meme-main.

The strongest open-source model, Qwen3-Omni, reaches only 55.4 and 57.4, respectively, and still lags behind Gemini 2.5 Flash, despite being considerably stronger than Gemma 3n, Qwen2.5-Omni, and phi-4-Multimodal.
For the audio-only, GPT-4o Audio remains the strongest, achieving an average accuracy of 50.1 on meme-main.

accuracies on meme-main are often 5–10% lower than on meme-full across all models and categories, showing that removing easy questions yields a more challenging evaluation that better tests genuine multimodal understanding.
audio-visual models consistently outperform their audio-only counterparts, confirming the benefit of visual signals for interpreting complex Internet clips
Across nearly all models, Language Analysis (L) is the easiest category, with leading systems such as Gemini 2.5 Flash, Qwen3-Omni, and GPT-4o Audio reaching 76–83% on meme-main.
Among these, W is the most difficult for most models, typically falling in the 20–55% range, while U also remains low across both audio-only and audio-visual models.
while MLLMs excel in surface semantic parsing, contextual, cultural, and pragmatic understanding still remains challenging.
Even the strongest audio LLMs, such as GPT-4o and Music Flamingo, reach only 35 to 45% on music and sound effects, compared with around 60 to 65% on speech and songs.
Japanese, Korean, and Persian are substantially more difficult, with leading models frequently dropping to the 35–55% range and audio-only LLMs sometimes falling below 30%
Even Gemini 3 pro only scores 56.1% in Persian on meme-main.
we recruit 20 participants, 10 native English speakers and 10 native Chinese speakers aged 18–35, all self-reported frequent Internet users.
This narrows to 750 memes in total and 37.5 memes per person.
As expected, humans perform much better on their familiar memes, outperforming all open-source MLLMs and comparable to Gemini 2.5 Flash.
Qwen3-Omni, the strongest open-source model, only slightly outperforms a human individual when we count the memes they have not seen.
high thinking improves AVG accuracy by 5.4% in the audio-only setting and 1.7% in the audio-visual setting on meme-main.

when we provide the name of the meme (written by the contributor, which often contains the song title, character name, or the meme itself), model accuracy increases significantly (≈10%) because many solutions become recallable from the LLM training text, bypassing audio/video understanding.

allowing visual-cheat conditions, i.e., keeping videos that disclose key information, causes substantial accuracy inflation, 40% or more on the visual-cheatable subset (numbers in parentheses), because on-screen text, titles, or visual objects directly reveal the answer.

cultural coverage is inevitably shaped by our contributors, who are highly-educated researchers aged 22–35 and whose perspectives do not fully represent the global, intergenerational landscape of meme culture.
Our annotations capture contemporary (by the end of 2025) interpretations and cannot anticipate future cultural drift (which is impossible).
most current MLLMs impose strict audio and video length limits, requiring clips to be truncated to 30 seconds, which may omit context essential for real-world understanding.
our evaluation focuses on controlled multiple-choice Q&A on single clips, whereas real-world applications often require multi-turn dialogue, personalization, and open-ended scenarios.

meme interpretation is inherently subjective. Although viewers may converge on a majority understanding, alternative readings are equally valid and cannot be fully reflected in a standardized benchmark.
AVMeme Exam should be viewed as a reference benchmark, diagnostic and comparative, rather than an absolute ground truth for human multimedia culture.
Human evaluation was conducted under an Institutional Review Board (IRB) protocol.
All participants completed the evaluation online in approximately 30 minutes and were compensated $15.
The benchmark is intended for research and evaluation, not for safety-critical or high-stakes deployment
